The gap between the actual output and the desired one is the error, or loss, and a calculus-based procedure called backpropagation works out how to nudge every weight so the error shrinks a little. Repeat across the whole collection, thousands of times over, and performance climbs.

The real prize comes afterward: shown a validation set of images it has never encountered, a well-trained network still gets them right. It has absorbed the statistical fingerprint of 'cat' — that is generalization, and it is why such systems can be turned loose on data no human has labeled, from photo libraries to medical scans.

steps.prompt: A network scores perfectly on its training images but performs at chance on new ones. What went wrong — and what result would have convinced you it genuinely learned the categories?
steps.reveal: It failed to generalize. Success on the training set only shows the weights have been tuned to those particular images — the network may have latched onto features specific to them rather than the distribution of features shared by the whole category. Genuine learning shows up one way: accuracy on the validation set, examples the network has never seen. Generalization is the entire point, which is why performance is judged on new data rather than on the material used for training.

steps.body:
The brain analogy is a loan, not a blueprint. The traffic runs in both directions. The layered, feature-stacking design of ANNs echoes the feature detectors Hubel and Wiesel uncovered, and neuroscientists use the same kind of pattern-learning machinery in reverse — training programs to decode what a person is viewing from their brain activity alone (Haxby et al., 2001).

Still, 'loosely based on the brain' is the honest phrase. A unit is a bare piece of arithmetic, while a real neuron is a living cell signaling chemically across synapses. And much of the recent explosion in ANN performance came from engineering, not neuroscience: GPUs — chips originally built for rendering game graphics — that compute enormous numbers of connection weights in parallel, plus huge open datasets to learn from, like ImageNet's 14+ million hand-annotated images spanning more than 20,000 object categories.

The field keeps moving, too. The classifiers we have discussed are discriminative models — they sort existing data into categories. Generative models instead learn a category's statistical structure well enough to create new examples: photorealistic faces of people who do not exist, or images conjured from a sentence of text.

The honest summary: ANNs prove that neuron-like arithmetic can learn flexible, cognition-like feats. That is a genuine clue about brains — not a portrait of one.

steps.q: When an artificial neural network learns to recognize cats, what actually changes inside it?
options: New nodes are added to store each cat it encounters
A programmer refines the if-then rules after each mistake
Its connection weights are gradually adjusted to reduce error on the training examples
Its activation function is swapped for a more accurate one
steps.explain: The architecture and activation function stay fixed, and no human writes recognition rules. Learning is nothing but incremental weight adjustment driven by the error signal — which mirrors the leading account of biological learning: change the synapses, change the mind.

title: Why a chalk drawing can open a hole in the sidewalk
blurb: sensation vs perception, transduction, receptor families, the poverty of the neural code, perception as active inference

steps.body:
You have never seen the world; you have only seen your brain's best guess about it.
Street artists exploit this. A skilled chalk artist can make flat pavement appear to drop away into a gaping pit, and pedestrians will step around it — even though every ray of light reaching their eyes came from level concrete. The physics was flat; the experience had depth.
That gap is the subject here. What we casually call 'seeing' is really two stages. Sensation is the body registering physical energy — light, pressure, vibration, chemicals — and converting it into neural signals. Perception is the brain interpreting those signals into an experienced world of objects, surfaces, and events. The chalk pit proves the two stages can disagree.

Transduction is the moment the physical world becomes a neural message.
Wrap your hand around a warm mug. Nerve endings in your skin respond to the heat and pressure by changing their firing rate — more stimulation, more action potentials per second. This conversion of physical energy into a neural code is called transduction, and it is the entry ticket for every sense.
Different receptor families handle different physics: mechanoreceptors respond to force (touch, blood pressure, vibrations in the inner ear), chemoreceptors to molecules (smell, taste), thermoreceptors to heat and cold, and photoreceptors to light. Photoreceptors are the oddballs — more light makes them release less neurotransmitter, the reverse of their cousins.
Notice what the brain actually receives from all this: not pictures, not sounds — just streams of spike rates. Everything you experience gets reconstructed from that.

steps.prompt: Reach into a bag, grab an unfamiliar object, and within a second you know it's a stapler. What did your skin actually deliver to your brain?
choices: A miniature 3D model of the stapler, assembled by receptors in the fingertips
Millions of separate local readings of pressure and temperature, encoded as firing rates
The word 'stapler', retrieved by specialized naming receptors in the hand
A single summary signal meaning 'hard metal object'
steps.reveal: The skin can only report what happens at each tiny patch — this spot pressed, that spot cool. The shape, the hinge, the identity 'stapler' are nowhere in the input. Your brain built them by combining millions of local measurements and matching the pattern against objects it has met before. That construction step is perception — and it takes a huge share of your cortex to pull off.

steps.body:
The senses hand the brain far less than the brain wants to know.
The eye's output is essentially an enormous spreadsheet: on the order of a hundred million entries, each a reading of how much light landed at one spot on the retina. Flat, noisy numbers. What you experience, though, is a three-dimensional room full of nameable things at particular distances. Nothing in the spreadsheet says 'coffee cup, arm's reach, handle facing left' — that must be inferred.
And the five outward-facing senses — exteroception — aren't the whole roster. You also carry senses aimed at your own body, called interoception: proprioception reports where your limbs are without looking, nociception signals tissue damage as pain, and equilibrioception keeps you upright. Close your eyes and touch your nose — proprioception just did that.

steps.prompt: An experiment you can run right now (gently!). Close one eye and press softly on the outer corner of the closed eyelid with a fingertip. Before you try: if perception simply reported the physical world, what should you experience? What do you predict actually happens?
steps.reveal: Most people see a faint glowing blob or ring — a phosphene — even though the room's light never changed. Pressure mechanically stimulates the retina, and the brain interprets any activity arriving on that pathway as light, because light is what retinal signals normally mean. What you perceive depends on which neural pathway is active, not on what actually stimulated it. The brain reads the code; it never touches the world directly.

steps.body:
Perception is active inference: a running bet about what is out there.
Any pattern of sensory input is compatible with many possible worlds. A flat chalk drawing and a genuine pit can paint nearly identical images on your retina — so the brain must gamble, and it gambles using experience. Hermann von Helmholtz (1867) called this unconscious inference: perception behaves like a conclusion drawn from evidence, except the reasoning is silent and instant.
The bets are usually so good you never notice them. Your eyes leap around several times a second, smearing wildly different images across the retina, yet you experience a rock-steady room. Two eyes receive two different images, yet you see one world. When the gamble occasionally fails — a chalk pit, a mirage — you get a rare look at the machinery.

steps.q: While your phone sits silent on the table across the room, you distinctly feel it buzz in your pocket — a 'phantom vibration.' Which claim does this best support?
options: Mechanoreceptors in the leg fire randomly, so sensation is fundamentally unreliable
Perceptual experience is constructed by the brain and can occur without a matching physical stimulus
Transduction can happen in the brain as well as in the skin
Interoception and exteroception share the same receptors
steps.explain: The buzz was an experience with no corresponding energy at the skin — a construction, almost certainly seeded by expectation. Random receptor noise wouldn't reliably feel like a phone, in the exact pocket where your phone lives. Sensation registers physical events; perception is the brain's interpretation, and interpretation can run ahead of the evidence. That gap between registering energy and constructing experience is the core distinction.

title: Why a faint star vanishes when you stare straight at it
blurb: cornea to retina, rods and cones, receptive fields, the visual hierarchy, dorsal and ventral streams, tonotopic and body maps

steps.body:
The eye is less a camera than a survey team with a tight budget.
Try this on a clear night: find a very faint star and look straight at it — it vanishes. Glance slightly to the side and it reappears. A camera would never do that; whatever sits at the center of its frame is captured best. Something about the eye's center is different, and it is a clue to how the whole instrument is built.
Light enters through the cornea, a clear layer that bends the light so it lands on the right part of the back of the eye, passes through the pupil — an adjustable hole in the colored iris — and lands on the retina, sheets of neurons lining the back of the eyeball. Because light travels in straight lines through a small opening, the image arrives upside down, and distant objects cast smaller images than near ones — a geometric fact the brain later recycles as a depth cue.

Two receptor types split the labor: one for starlight, one for daylight and detail.
Rods are extremely light-sensitive but colorblind and coarse; they populate the retina's periphery. Cones demand plenty of light but deliver sharp detail and — because they come in three wavelength-tuned varieties — color; they are crammed into the fovea, the retina's center, which handles whatever you aim your gaze at.
That solves the star mystery: staring puts the dim star on cone territory, and cones can't respond to so little light. Looking slightly away drops it onto rod territory, where it registers.
The retina also edits before it ships. Its layered circuitry compresses the signal — think of an image file being shrunk before upload — because everything must exit through the optic nerve, a cable of axons kept slim so the eye can still swivel freely.

steps.prompt: You're out stargazing and want to catch a faint meteor streak. Given the retina's wiring, what's the best strategy?
choices: Stare at the exact spot you expect it — the fovea has the densest packing of receptors
Watch slightly off-center, letting the sensitive rods of the periphery do the work
Blink rapidly to keep refreshing the photoreceptors
Cover one eye, since binocular input dilutes dim signals
steps.reveal: The fovea is dense, but with cones — high resolution, low sensitivity. In dim conditions the periphery's rods are your best detectors, which is why astronomers deliberately practice 'averted vision.' Receptor type, not receptor count, decides what you can see in the dark.

steps.body:
Every visual neuron monitors one small patch of the world — and cares about something specific happening there.
The region of sensory space that can change a neuron's firing is its receptive field. Recording from cat cortex, David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel (1959) found that neurons in the primary visual cortex (V1) mostly ignore diffuse light but fire enthusiastically when an edge at one particular angle crosses their patch — a tilted line here, a vertical bar there.
From the retina, signals pass through the thalamus's lateral geniculate nucleus to V1, then onward through dozens of cortical regions. The organization is hierarchical: each stage responds to more complex and more specific things than the one before. V1 wants oriented edges; mid-level areas want contours and shapes; late regions in the temporal lobe hold neurons keen on faces, places, or whole objects. The fusiform face area activates strongly for faces (Kanwisher et al., 1997) — though Gauthier and Tarr (1997) showed it also fires for any category you've become a visual expert in, even invented lab creatures called Greebles, keeping the 'face area vs expertise area' debate alive.

steps.prompt: Patient D.F. has damage to her ventral visual stream. Asked to describe or match the tilt of a slot in front of her, she answers almost at random — as if she cannot see orientation at all. Now she's handed a card and asked to actually post it through that slot. Predict: does she succeed?
steps.reveal: She nails it — rotating the card to the slot's angle in one smooth motion. Goodale and Milner (1991) argued this exposes a division of labor: the damaged ventral stream (into the temporal lobe) serves conscious perception — recognizing and reporting what things are — while her intact dorsal stream (into the parietal lobe) guides action in real time. A patient with the reverse damage shows the mirror-image pattern: fluent at describing, clumsy at grasping. Vision is not one system; it is at least two, split by what the information is for.

steps.body:
Every other sense runs the same three-step play: transduce, relay, map.
Hearing: the outer ear funnels vibrations down the canal to the eardrum and three tiny bones, which amplify them into the fluid-filled cochlea. There, hair cells — mechanoreceptors bent by the fluid's motion — perform transduction. They sit in a tonotopic map: position along the cochlea's coil corresponds to sound frequency, an ordering preserved all the way up to auditory cortex.
Touch: skin mechanoreceptors project to the somatosensory cortex, where Wilder Penfield described the homunculus — a body map with gloriously wrong proportions. Fingertips and lips, dense with receptors, claim huge cortical territory; the receptor-sparse trunk gets a sliver. More incoming detail earns more processing acreage.
Smell and taste run on chemoreceptors; the smell signal reaches the olfactory bulb, which links directly to the amygdala and hippocampus — a plausible reason a stray scent can ambush you with a decades-old memory.

steps.q: An experimenter finds a neuron that fires strongly whenever a face appears — any face, any size, almost anywhere in view — but barely responds to bars, edges, or scrambled face parts. Where in the visual pathway is this neuron most plausibly located?
options: The retina, since faces are biologically urgent stimuli
V1, whose neurons have the most precisely tuned receptive fields
Late in the ventral stream's hierarchy, where responses are complex, specific, and tolerant of position and size
The optic nerve, which carries all facial information to the brain
steps.explain: Position- and size-tolerant responses to a complex category are the signature of late hierarchical stages. Retinal and V1 neurons have small receptive fields tuned to simple properties — local light change, edge orientation — so a face detector there is impossible. The hierarchy principle (simple and local early, complex and invariant late) is the discriminating idea.

title: The cough that ate a syllable
blurb: bottom-up and top-down processing, Helmholtz's unconscious inference, Gibson's perception-action loop, Gestalt grouping laws

steps.body:
Your brain routinely hears sounds that never reached your ears.
Play someone a recorded sentence in which one syllable has been snipped out and replaced with a cough. Listeners don't report a gap — they hear the complete word with a cough layered on top. This is the phonemic restoration effect, and the missing sound was manufactured entirely by the listener's brain.
It is the perfect specimen for a key distinction. Bottom-up processing works purely from the incoming signal — general-purpose operations applied to whatever arrives, no knowledge of what the stimulus is. Top-down processing recruits knowledge and expectation from beyond the stimulus: your vocabulary told you which syllable belonged in that slot, so your brain penciled it in. Real perception is a constant negotiation between the two.

steps.prompt: Which of these is the clearest case of top-down processing?
choices: Retinal circuits flagging locations where brightness changes sharply
Hair cells along the cochlea sorting a sound into its component frequencies
Deciphering a friend's terrible handwriting because only one word could fit that sentence
Your pupil constricting when you step out into sunlight
steps.reveal: Edge detection, frequency sorting, and pupil reflexes run identically for every stimulus — signal-driven and knowledge-free, so bottom-up. The handwriting case imports something not present in the ink: your knowledge of the language and the sentence's meaning. Whenever information beyond the stimulus shapes what you perceive, that's top-down.

steps.body:
Helmholtz: what you perceive is a conclusion — you just never witness the reasoning.
Spot a furry tail poking out one side of the couch and an ear over the top, and you perceive a cat behind the couch — not two disconnected cat fragments. No whole cat exists in your retinal image; you inferred it.
Hermann von Helmholtz (1867) built this into the constructive theory of perception: the brain uses sensory evidence to assemble an internal model of the world, and behavior is aimed at the model, not at the raw input. He named the process unconscious inference — automatic, silent, and irresistible.
His evidence still holds up: your eyes jump several times a second, yet the world appears perfectly still; each eye receives a measurably different image, yet you perceive a single scene. Something is clearly building one stable model out of unstable input.

Gibson's rebuttal: why build a model when the light already tells you what to do?
James J. Gibson argued for direct perception: organisms don't reconstruct the world internally — they pick up information available in the stimulus itself and let it steer behavior in a continuous perception-action loop. Walking toward a doorway? No need to compute its coordinates in three dimensions; keep its image centered and expanding in your view, correct when it drifts, and you will arrive.
The lineage is telling. Physiologist Johannes Müller had proposed direct nerve routes from sensation to behavior; his own student Helmholtz broke away, insisting the signals must first be combined into something model-like. Psychology has been staging that argument ever since.

steps.prompt: An outfielder sprints to catch a high fly ball. The constructive account says her brain computes the ball's 3D landing spot, then she runs there. A direct account says she runs so as to keep the ball's image moving in a simple, predictable way in her visual field, correcting continuously. What does each theory predict about the shape of her running path — and which would you bet on?
steps.reveal: Computing a landing point in advance predicts a straight dash to a fixed destination. Continuous optical control predicts a path that bends as she corrects on the fly — no landing-point calculation ever required. Gibson's claim is that much skilled behavior works this second way: the stimulus itself carries enough information to steer action, with no internal model as middleman. But bi-stable figures, illusions, and the stable visual world are hard to explain without internal models. Many researchers treat the theories as describing complementary systems — model-building for recognizing and reporting, direct control for fast action — an echo of the ventral/dorsal split.

steps.body:
The Gestalt movement mapped the rules by which fragments become wholes.
Stars are scattered points, yet people across cultures see hunters, bears, and ladles up there. Over a hundred years ago, the Gestalt psychologists catalogued the grouping principles behind this, calling them laws of perceptual organization.
The law of similarity: elements alike in color or form group together — dots of alternating colors organize into stripes. The law of proximity: elements near one another group — nine musicians standing in three tight clusters read as three units, not nine. Good continuation: elements along a smooth path group — two crossing lines look like an X made of two straight strokes, never four bent ones meeting at a point.
These laws are not arbitrary decoration; they are statistics about real objects absorbed into the machinery. Parts of one object usually are similar, nearby, and smoothly contoured. Gestalt grouping is unconscious inference with the assumptions baked in — a quiet bridge back to Helmholtz.

steps.q: Which experimental finding would provide the strongest support for direct perception over the constructive theory?
options: People perceive a stable world even though their eyes jump several times per second
A person accurately guides skilled actions using vision while being unable to describe or recognize the very properties guiding them
Observers watching an ambiguous cube see it flip between two 3D interpretations
Listeners' knowledge of words changes which speech sounds they report hearing
steps.explain: The stable world, flipping cubes, and word-driven hearing are showcase evidence for internal models and knowledge-driven construction. Vision guiding action without any reportable percept — as in patient D.F. — shows visual control of behavior running without a conscious model as middleman, exactly the perception-action loop direct perception describes. Knowing which phenomena demand a model and which don't is the live scientific question.

title: The two gray squares your brain refuses to match
blurb: lightness constancy, the Adelson checkerboard, depth cues, stereopsis, the hollow face, the invariance problem, context effects

steps.body:
An illusion is the brain's assumptions caught in the act.
Vision scientist Edward Adelson's checkerboard is the classic. A cylinder casts a shadow across a checkered surface; square A sits outside the shadow and looks dark, square B inside it and looks light. Measure the actual light coming from each and they are pixel-for-pixel identical — your photoreceptors respond to them identically. Yet no act of will makes them match.
Why? Because your visual system isn't reporting light; it is estimating reflectance — the stable surface property of how much light a thing bounces back. A black backpack in sunlight can send your eye thousands of times more light than white paper indoors, so raw light readings are nearly useless for judging surfaces. The brain discounts the illumination it infers: 'B is in shadow yet still sending this much light, so its surface must be pale.' The drive toward stable surface estimates is called lightness constancy — it is why your backpack reliably looks black everywhere, and it only misfires here because Adelson engineered the scene.

steps.prompt: In the checkerboard illusion, why does square B (inside the shadow) look lighter than the physically identical square A?
choices: B genuinely reflects more light into the eye, and the brain reports that accurately
Cones in the fovea adapt to shadow faster than rods do
The brain infers B is dimly lit, so a surface sending that much light from within shadow must be a pale one
Squares adjacent to curved objects always appear lighter
steps.reveal: The two squares deliver identical light — sensation cannot tell them apart. The difference is injected at the interpretation stage: cues in the scene (the cylinder, the soft-edged shadow) convince your brain that B sits under weaker illumination, so it credits B's surface with higher reflectance. What you perceive is the brain's estimate of the surface, not the raw measurement.

steps.body:
Depth is never in the image — it is always inferred from clues.
The retina is a 2D sheet; distance is the dimension the optics throw away. The brain recovers it from converging cues. Occlusion: whatever blocks another object is closer. Relative size: farther objects cast smaller retinal images. Motion parallax: as you move, near things sweep across your view faster than far ones — fence posts blur past the train window while mountains crawl.
The heavyweight cue is binocular disparity. Your eyes sit a couple of inches apart and receive slightly different images; how far a feature's position differs between the two retinas depends on its depth relative to where you're fixating. Hold up a finger, alternate winking, and watch it jump against the background. The brain converts these disparities into vivid depth — an ability called stereopsis.
It has to be learned: infants develop it around crawling age, and if the eyes can't be aligned during early childhood, stereopsis may never arrive. Close one eye, though, and the world only flattens a little — the other cues carry on.

steps.prompt: A rotating mask of a face turns so that you are now viewing its hollow back — the concave inside, like the interior of a mold. Shading and disparity all say 'concave.' Predict what you will actually perceive, and why.
steps.reveal: Nearly everyone sees a normal convex face popping outward, nose toward the viewer — the famous hollow face illusion. Bottom-up depth cues correctly signal concavity, but a lifetime of faces — every one of them convex — supplies a top-down expectation so strong it overrules the geometry. Even depth, which feels like raw data, is a negotiated verdict, and category knowledge can outvote the evidence. The Necker cube makes a matching point from the opposite direction: when evidence is perfectly balanced between two 3D readings, perception flips back and forth — the brain revising its guess in real time.

steps.body:
The obvious theory of recognition — match the image to a stored snapshot — fails immediately.
A template model says: keep an image of each known object in memory and compare new input to it point by point. But you never receive the same image twice. Viewpoint, distance, lighting, and pose reshuffle every pixel: four photos of one woman — full face, each profile, back of the head — share almost nothing at the image level, yet you effortlessly know they show one person. Recognizing an object across radically different images of it is the invariance problem, and it is the central difficulty of recognition.
It comes in two flavors. Identification: same individual across views. Classification: a creature you have never encountered — some elegant, long-nosed breed — is still instantly 'dog,' even though no stored snapshot covers a first meeting.
The escape route researchers pursue is features. A 'K' printed in four eccentric fonts shares no pixels across versions, but each has a tall stroke with two diagonals branching off. Find properties that survive the variation and recognition becomes possible — though discovering the right features for real-world objects has proved brutally hard.

Recognition never happens in a vacuum — the scene votes too.
An identical smudged scribble reads as a 'B' in one sentence and an 'R' in another, purely because of the words around it. Objects get the same treatment from their surroundings.
Irving Biederman (1972) showed that people recognize an object faster and more accurately when it appears in a sensible setting than when it is dropped into the wrong one. Barenholtz (2014) pushed further: participants identified photographed objects at far lower resolution when context was present — and lower still when the context was their own home. We carry scene schemas, knowledge of what belongs where, and we lean on them constantly.
This is top-down processing closing the recognition loop: kitchens make toasters easier to see. The blurrier or more ambiguous the input, the more the surroundings decide the verdict.

steps.q: A security system stores one reference photo of each employee's face and verifies people by pixel-by-pixel comparison with the camera feed. It fails constantly. Which idea best explains why?
options: Figure-ground assignment: the system cannot separate faces from background
The invariance problem: one object produces radically different images across viewpoint, lighting, and expression, so snapshot matching cannot generalize
Motion parallax: employees walk through the door at different speeds
Lightness constancy: the system perceives reflectance instead of luminance
steps.explain: This system is the template model rebuilt in software, and it fails for the template model's reason: the same face never sends the same image twice. Human recognition survives that variation — evidence that we rely on something more abstract than stored snapshots, such as variation-tolerant features plus context. Seeing why templates cannot solve the invariance problem is the discriminating idea.

title: The sticker that turns a banana into a toaster
blurb: convolution kernels, feature maps, learned feature hierarchies, parallels to visual cortex, adversarial examples, texture bias

steps.body:
A convolution is a tiny feature detector swept across an image.
Picture a stencil of a diagonal stroke that you drag over a photo one patch at a time. At each stop you check how well the patch beneath matches the stencil's pattern; a perfect overlap scores high, a mismatch scores near zero. That is a convolution: a small grid of numbers — the kernel — is multiplied against each region of the image and the results summed, yielding a large value wherever the image locally resembles the kernel.
Sweep the kernel across every position and you get a feature map: a new image whose bright spots mean 'the feature lives here.' Notice the quiet superpower: one detector finds its feature at any location. That is a first bite out of the invariance problem that sinks template models — a diagonal is a diagonal wherever it lands.

Nobody hand-designs the detectors — the network learns them from its mistakes.
In 1966, MIT's Seymour Papert famously handed computer vision to his graduate students as a summer project. The summer stretched into five decades. Human-engineered features could read zip codes and inspect factory parts, but general recognition of everyday objects stayed out of reach — hand-picking the right features is precisely the problem that stumps theorists of human vision too.
A convolutional neural network (CNN) sidesteps it: kernel values are just connection weights, and the network nudges them repeatedly to shrink its labeling errors over a mountain of example images. Stack layers so that later kernels convolve the earlier feature maps, and features compound: two diagonal detectors combine into an X detector; edges become corners and textures, textures become parts, parts become whole objects. Complexity is assembled, layer by layer, out of simplicity.

steps.prompt: A CNN is trained from random starting weights to recognize thousands of everyday photos. Afterward, researchers visualize what its first layer of kernels has learned to detect. What do they typically find?
choices: Miniature templates of whole objects — tiny faces, cars, and dogs
Oriented edges and simple contrasts, uncannily like the preferences Hubel and Wiesel found in V1 neurons
Nothing interpretable — the weights remain essentially random
Letters and digits, since those are the simplest human symbols
steps.reveal: Trained CNNs rediscover oriented edge detectors in their first layer — nobody puts them there. Deeper layers develop preferences for contours, then object parts, then whole categories, paralleling the biological hierarchy from V1 through the temporal lobe. Networks pressured toward sparse codes develop V1-like features especially closely — a hint that the brain itself may use a sparse encoding scheme. When two very different systems facing the same problem converge on the same solution, that is evidence about the problem itself: edge-first hierarchies may simply be how vision gets solved.

steps.body:
The successes are real: CNNs now handle recognition problems that stumped engineers for decades.
CNN-based systems flag tumors and other anomalies in medical scans, help steer vehicles, monitor crops, and pick your face out of a crowd for access control — a stunning turn for a problem that once seemed to require a brain.
The payoff runs both ways. Because a CNN is fully inspectable — every weight can be examined — it doubles as a working hypothesis about biological vision: a live demonstration that layered feature detection, learned from experience, can go a very long way toward recognizing objects. And the features these networks learn look strikingly like what real neurons respond to, from oriented edges early on to whole objects late — suggesting they have much to teach us about real brains.
But scoring like a human is not the same as seeing like one — and the differences are where things get interesting.

steps.prompt: Take a photo a CNN confidently labels 'panda.' Now add a whisper of carefully computed pixel noise — so faint that the altered photo looks utterly unchanged to every human who views it. Predict what happens to the CNN's answer, and what your prediction implies about how its recognition differs from yours.
steps.reveal: The network's label can flip to 'gibbon' — often with higher confidence than before (Szegedy et al., 2014; Goodfellow et al., 2015). These adversarial examples reveal that the CNN's decision rides on fragile, high-frequency statistical patterns no human uses or notices. Physical versions exist too: a small printed sticker placed next to a banana made a network report 'toaster' (Brown et al., 2017). Human vision has no known counterpart to this failure — our recognition tracks shape, parts, and context, which faint pixel dust doesn't disturb. Matching human accuracy is not the same as using human strategy.

steps.body:
Where CNNs and people part ways, each difference is a clue about human vision.
Robert Geirhos and colleagues (2019) built chimeras — a cat's silhouette rendered in elephant-skin texture. People overwhelmingly say 'cat'; standard CNNs say 'elephant.' The networks lean on texture; humans weigh global shape. Retrained to prefer shape, networks become more robust — the human strategy turns out to be the sturdier one.
Other gaps: CNNs typically need millions of labeled examples where a child needs a handful; they crumble under distribution shift — rain, odd poses, unfamiliar clutter — where humans shrug; and a plain feedforward CNN has no top-down channel, no scene schema whispering that toasters live in kitchens, no expectation to fill in an occluded contour.
So the model earns its keep twice. Its successes show how far pure bottom-up feature hierarchies can go; its failures mark, almost surgically, what the rest of human perception — priors, context, inference — is adding on top.

steps.q: A CNN matches human accuracy on a standard image benchmark, yet imperceptible pixel noise flips its labels, and cat-shaped objects with elephant texture fool it. What is the best conclusion?
options: The network needs more layers before it will behave like a brain
Human vision must be equally vulnerable — we simply haven't found our own adversarial examples yet
Equal accuracy came from different strategies: the network exploits texture and fragile statistical cues, while human recognition rests on shape, context, and inference
Benchmarks understate CNN ability, since pixel noise and texture chimeras never occur in real scenes
steps.explain: A matching benchmark score only shows the outputs agree on that image distribution — not that the mechanisms agree. Failure modes are the diagnostic: they expose which cues each system actually relies on, and here they diverge sharply. That is why a model's errors, compared against human errors, are scientifically precious — they reveal exactly what the model lacks and what human vision quietly contributes.

title: Why one voice survives a loud party
blurb: Limited capacity, selective attention, the cocktail-party effect, dichotic listening and shadowing.

steps.body:
Your senses collect far more than your brain can use. Right now each of your eyes is streaming something like a hundred million light readings, refreshed dozens of times a second - and that is one sense out of many, before you count sound, touch, and everything your body reports from the inside.
A brain of finite size cannot compute all of it. Something has to choose which trickle of that flood gets deep processing and which gets dropped. That choosing is attention. William James (1890) opened his account with the line "Everyone knows what attention is" - the felt experience of the mind taking hold of one thing and letting the rest fall away.

Attention behaves like a funnel with a narrow spout. Sit in a crowded restaurant: dozens of conversations physically reach your ears, but only one reaches you. The rest blur into murmur.
Committing to one stream of input at the expense of all the others is selective attention, and its most famous everyday demonstration is the cocktail-party effect: locking onto a single voice in a room full of competing voices. A useful image is a spotlight on a dark stage - whatever falls in the beam is vivid, and everything outside it barely exists for you.

steps.prompt: You spend twenty minutes locked into one conversation at a party while another conversation runs continuously two tables away. Predict what you could report about that ignored conversation afterward - the topic, specific words, anything at all?
steps.reveal: Almost nothing about content. Cherry (1953) found that listeners could say whether an ignored voice was male or female, but not what it said - even a switch into German, or speech played backward, routinely went unnoticed. Coarse physical features survive the filter; meaning mostly does not.

steps.body:
The party effect can be bottled and studied with headphones. In dichotic listening (Cherry, 1953), a different spoken message plays into each ear. The listener must shadow one ear - repeat its words aloud in real time - which forces attention onto that channel and lets researchers probe what leaked in from the other one.
The leakage is remarkably small. Moray (1959) played the same words as many as thirty times into the ignored ear; afterward, listeners showed no recognition of those words at all. Whatever the filter does, it does it thoroughly.

steps.prompt: In shadowing experiments, which change in the ignored ear were listeners most likely to actually notice?
choices: The language switching from English to German
The same word repeating dozens of times
The voice switching from male to female
The topic changing mid-sentence
steps.reveal: Physical characteristics - pitch, gender, a voice becoming a pure tone - penetrate the filter and get noticed. Content-level changes like language, repetition, or topic sail past unregistered (Cherry, 1953; Moray, 1959). That asymmetry is the central clue about what unattended input does and does not receive.

steps.q: A friend insists she takes in every conversation at a busy party. Based on dichotic listening research, what does she most plausibly retain from the conversations she is not following?
options: Coarse physical features like voice pitch or gender, but little or no meaning
The full meaning of each conversation, stored but hard to retrieve
Nothing whatsoever, as if the sound never reached her ears
The meaning of every sentence, but only for about one second
steps.explain: Unattended sound is fully transduced by the ears and analyzed for surface features, but its meaning mostly never gets computed. Selection exists because processing capacity - not hearing - is the bottleneck.

title: How your name sneaks past a blocked ear
blurb: Broadbent's early filter, breakthrough by meaning, Treisman's attenuator, late selection, Lavie's load theory.

steps.body:
The real debate is where the filter sits, not whether one exists. Your inner ears transduce every conversation within earshot - attention cannot switch the ears off. The blocking happens somewhere downstream, in the brain. So how far does an ignored voice travel before it is dropped?
Early selection answers: not far. In Broadbent's (1958) filter model, the flood of input is held briefly in a sensory buffer, and a filter passes just one channel - chosen by physical properties like pitch or location - onward to the stage that computes meaning. On this view an ignored conversation is never understood at all, which is exactly why you cannot recall it later.

steps.prompt: If Broadbent is right and ignored speech never reaches the meaning stage, what should happen when someone in the ignored channel speaks your name? Make a prediction before revealing.
steps.reveal: Strict early selection predicts nothing should happen - a name is just meaning, and meaning was never computed. But Moray (1959) found names often break through and grab the listener. Gray and Wedderburn (1960) found something stranger: when a story hopped between ears ("Dear Aunt Jane..." alternating with numbers), people followed the story across ears despite instructions to stick to one. Both results require that the ignored ear's content was understood at least partially - a direct problem for a filter that blocks meaning entirely.

steps.body:
Two rescue attempts: move the filter late, or turn it into a volume knob. Late selection models propose that every input gets basic semantic analysis first, and only then does selection happen - the losers are simply forgotten fast.
Treisman (1964) proposed a subtler fix: attenuation. The ignored channel is not severed, it is turned down - like a phone call over a weak signal, degraded but still partly there. That weakened signal still gets identified whenever it hits an entry with a hair-trigger threshold: your own name, or a word the surrounding context makes highly predictable.

steps.prompt: Mackay (1973) had people attend to ambiguous sentences like "The boys threw rocks at the bank" while the ignored ear repeated the word "money." Listeners later interpreted the sentence as the financial kind of bank - yet denied ever hearing "money." What does this show?
choices: Ignored input can be semantically processed enough to bias interpretation, without ever reaching awareness
The ignored word was consciously heard and then quickly repressed
Ambiguous words always default to their financial meaning
Shadowing blocks all processing of the attended sentence
steps.reveal: The meaning of "money" got in and did work - it steered comprehension - while consciousness never came along for the ride. Unconscious semantic influence is hard to square with a strict early filter, and it suggests the filter is leakier and more flexible than Broadbent's original model allowed.

steps.body:
Whether a distractor gets processed depends on how busy you are. In the flanker task of Eriksen and Eriksen (1974), you identify a center letter while ignoring letters beside it. When the flanking letters call for the opposite response, you slow down - proof you processed them even though you knew exactly where to look and wanted to ignore them.
This introduces attentional load: how much of your limited processing capacity the current task consumes. A demanding task and an easy task may leave very different amounts of capacity lying around.

Lavie's load theory: perception is a tank that fills - and spills. Lavie (1995) had people hunt for a target letter in either an easy, uniform ring (low load) or a hard, jumbled ring (high load), with an irrelevant flanker off to the side. The incompatible flanker slowed people only in the low-load condition.
Her reading: an easy task leaves spare capacity, and spare capacity gets spent involuntarily - it spills onto the distractor, so filtering looks late. A hard task drains the tank, nothing is left for the flanker, and filtering looks early. Think of the crinkly snack bag at the movies: it torments you during a slow scene and vanishes during a gripping one. Early versus late stops being a war and becomes a dial.

steps.q: Absorbed in a genuinely demanding puzzle, you do not register the TV chatter nearby at all. Later, idly sorting socks, the same chatter keeps intruding. Load theory says this happened because...
options: your hearing sensitivity physically drops during hard tasks
the filter always operates late, regardless of what you are doing
the demanding puzzle consumed your full perceptual capacity, leaving none for the chatter - while the easy task left spare capacity that spilled onto it
boredom during easy tasks amplifies the loudness of sounds
steps.explain: Lavie (1995): spare perceptual capacity is allocated whether you want it or not. Distractor processing tracks the load of your current task - which is why the attentional filter behaves early under high load and late under low load.

title: Why hands-free calls don't fix distracted driving
blurb: Divided attention, dual-task costs, automaticity, task switching, driving-and-phone research.

steps.body:
Doing two things at once usually means doing both worse. Picture reading a dense article while a group chat pings every minute - each reply feels quick, yet the article somehow takes twice as long. Fox, Rosen, and Crawford (2009) measured exactly this: students who kept up instant messages during a reading task were significantly slower to get through it.
Spreading processing across multiple tasks at the same time is divided attention - everyday multitasking. Because attentional resources are finite, splitting them produces measurable dual-task costs.

steps.prompt: Many places banned handheld phones while driving, on the theory that the danger is a hand off the wheel. Predict: does switching to a hands-free setup eliminate the impairment?
steps.reveal: No - and that is the pivotal result. Strayer and Johnston (2001) found phone conversations made simulated drivers nearly twice as likely to miss red lights and about 10% slower to brake, with no significant difference between handheld and hands-free. The cost lives in central processing resources, not in the hands. Strayer, Drews, and Crouch (2006) put the impairment in the same range as driving legally drunk.

steps.body:
Not all conversation costs the same. Drews et al. (2008) compared drivers chatting on a phone with drivers chatting with an in-car passenger: the phone group drifted out of their lane far more often.
Why the gap? Something appears uniquely demanding about the cell-phone conversation itself: error rates are similarly elevated for phone calls compared to merely listening to the radio or an audiobook (Strayer & Johnston, 2001). Holding up your end of a remote two-way exchange reallocates attentional resources away from the road in a way passive listening does not.

Practice can shrink a task's price - sometimes close to zero. Remember first learning to drive: pedal pressure, mirror checks, and steering angle each demanded deliberate thought. Years later, most of that runs with no conscious oversight. That is automaticity: with extensive practice, a task comes to need little or no attention.
Reading is the classic case. Stroop (1935) showed you cannot stop yourself from reading a word even when your only job is to name its ink color - decades of practice made word-reading run on its own, whether you want it to or not (MacLeod, 1991).

steps.prompt: An experienced driver argues: "Driving is automatic for me, so a phone call costs me nothing." Where exactly does this reasoning break down?
choices: Driving never becomes automatic to any degree
Phone conversations impair only novice drivers
It doesn't - practiced drivers show no dual-task costs
Automaticity reduces demands but does not erase them - and when something unexpected happens, demand spikes at the very moment the call has consumed the spare capacity
steps.reveal: Well-practiced driving still draws on the shared resource pool, and hazards arrive without warning, demanding everything at once. Worse, people reliably overestimate their own multitasking ability - confidence and competence come apart here.

steps.body:
Much of "multitasking" may really be rapid switching. One view says attention genuinely runs in parallel across tasks; a rival view says we alternate quickly, and the costs come from task switching - the brain needs time to reconfigure for each new task. Ironically, the people who multitask the most tend to show the largest switching costs, so a self-described great multitasker may be an especially poor one.
True simultaneity is not impossible everywhere, though: in multiple-object tracking, people can follow roughly four or five moving targets at once among distractors (Cowan, 2000; Intriligator & Cavanagh, 2001).

steps.q: Which finding most directly proves that the danger of phoning while driving is about central processing resources rather than hands on the wheel?
options: Drivers grip the wheel with both hands more when not on the phone
Passengers talk more than remote callers do
Handheld and hands-free phones impaired braking and light detection about equally (Strayer & Johnston, 2001)
Radio listening slightly improves driver mood
steps.explain: If the impairment were physical, freeing the hands would fix it. Equal impairment across handheld and hands-free localizes the cost to shared attentional resources consumed by the conversation itself - the signature of a dual-task cost.

title: Staring right at the coin and missing the switch
blurb: Posner cueing, the attentional spotlight, overt vs covert attention, feature binding, visual search, inattentional blindness.

steps.body:
Attention prepares processing before a stimulus even arrives. In Posner's (1980) cueing experiments, you fixate a central cross while an arrow hints where a target will probably appear - and your eyes never move. On valid trials (the cue points to where the target really shows up, 80% of the time), detection is reliably faster than on invalid trials.
The cue let attention pre-activate processing at that location, so the target landed on warmed-up machinery. A helpful image is a spotlight that can sweep ahead of the eyes, brightening one region of the scene while the rest stays dim.

steps.prompt: In Posner's experiments the eyes stayed glued to the central cross the entire time, yet valid cues still sped up detection. What does that detail isolate?
choices: Eye movements are faster than attention shifts
Attention can move to a location and enhance processing there independently of where the eyes are pointing
Peripheral vision has higher acuity than the fovea
Cues help only when you look straight at the cued location
steps.reveal: With gaze pinned, none of the speedup can come from the high-resolution fovea reaching the target. It must come from a covert shift of attention that readied the cued location in advance - attention and gaze are separable systems.

steps.body:
Attention usually rides with your gaze - but it can travel alone. Pointing your eyes at what you are attending is overt attention: it parks the target on the fovea, where detail is richest. Attending off to the side while your eyes stay put is covert attention - the poker player tracking an opponent without looking, or your visual system scouting the next landing spot an instant before the eyes jump. Covert attention is also socially useful, since gaze direction is easy for others to read and we do not always want to broadcast our interest.
What summons the spotlight in the first place? Sometimes the world does: a flashbulb or a siren captures attention exogenously, automatically. Sometimes you do: choosing to focus based on goals is endogenous control.

One core job of attention is gluing features together. Color, shape, and motion are handled by different brain regions - yet you see one purple triangle, never free-floating purpleness plus triangleness. Treisman's feature-integration theory holds that attention is the binder that welds separate features into single objects (Treisman & Gelade, 1980).
Remove attention and the welds fail. For stimuli they had not attended, people identifying simple shapes made predictable conjunction errors - remembering individual features correctly but pairing them wrongly, such as reporting a purple triangle and an orange oval that were never shown together that way (Treisman & Schmidt, 1982). The features were registered; the pairings were scrambled without attention to bind them.

steps.prompt: Search puzzle one: find the lone green bar among red bars. Search puzzle two: find the tilted red bar among upright red bars and tilted green bars. Predict which search slows down as more distractors are added - and why.
steps.reveal: Puzzle one shows pop-out: a single unique feature seizes attention no matter how big the crowd, so adding distractors barely costs anything. Puzzle two is conjunction search - the target is unique only in its combination of color and tilt, so you must attend items one by one, binding each item's features to check it, adding roughly 20-40 milliseconds per extra item. That linear cost is just what feature-integration theory predicts, though later work shows search can also be guided and partly parallel rather than purely item-by-item (Wolfe, Cave, & Franzel, 1989).

steps.body:
Whatever attention skips can vanish from awareness entirely. Inattentional blindness is failing to perceive something fully visible because it sits outside your attentional beam - viewers absorbed in counting how many times jump-ropers successfully jump can completely miss a chicken in the scene. Its cousin, change blindness, is failing to spot the difference between two alternating flashed images even across many repetitions.
Here is the unsettling part: looking is not enough. Spectators who tracked a coin closely through a magic routine still missed it being swapped for a different coin mid-trick (Smith, Lamont, & Henderson, 2012). And the effect is not just visual - a demanding visual task can make people miss clearly audible sounds, an inattentional deafness (Macdonald & Lavie, 2011).

steps.q: A magician swaps a coin while a spectator's eyes track it continuously - and the spectator still misses the swap. What is the sharpest lesson?
options: Fixating an object guarantees perceiving it, so the spectator must have blinked
Coins are too small for the fovea to resolve
The swap was perceived but instantly forgotten because coins carry no meaning
Conscious perception depends on attention, not merely on where the eyes point - gaze without attention is not enough
steps.explain: Change blindness under direct fixation shows the eye delivers data but attention decides what becomes a percept you actually experience. It is the mirror image of Posner's finding: there, attention worked without gaze; here, gaze fails without attention.

title: A brain zap that moved attention, not the eyes
blurb: Anticipatory pre-activation, parietal control of attention, endogenous vs exogenous networks, frontal eye fields, neglect and ADHD.

steps.body:
Attention turns up the gain in whichever sensory cortex is about to do the work. A sprinter waiting for the starting gun is a brain waiting too: auditory cortex ramps up before any sound arrives (Leaver et al., 2009). Expecting a visual event does the same for visual areas.
Shulman et al. (1999) showed this cleanly. An arrow cue told participants which direction a field of dots would move, and brain activity was recorded while they were still looking at the arrow, merely anticipating the motion. Motion-processing area MT was already more active than in a passive condition with no task. Attention prepares the relevant regions for activity - and that preparation begins before the stimulus exists.

steps.prompt: Shulman et al. (1999) also found the intraparietal sulcus active during anticipation - even though that region does not itself process motion. What is the best interpretation?
choices: The scan must have mislocalized area MT
Anticipation deactivates the parietal lobe
The parietal region is a control source: it modulates activity in sensory areas like MT rather than doing the sensory work itself
The intraparietal sulcus is secretly a motion-processing area
steps.reveal: The intraparietal sulcus is not essential for processing motion, so its activity points to a different job: the parietal lobe was modulating the activity of MT - controlling which portions of the brain are paying attention. The parietal cortex was conducting; MT was playing.

steps.body:
Two kinds of attention, two partially separable brain networks. Goal-directed, anticipation-based attention appears to run on different circuitry than exogenous, bottom-up attention (Corbetta & Shulman, 2002). Regions in the posterior parietal lobes serve as controllers, determining which other brain areas get activated for endogenous attention. Exogenous capture works differently: evidence points to right-hemisphere regions, notably the temporoparietal junction, whose job is snapping attention onto unexpected stimuli.
The two systems obviously must interact: hunting for your black car in a packed lot is goal-driven, yet that very goal gives every black vehicle in view increased salience to your visual system.

Where the two networks meet: the frontal eye fields. An important region for their interaction is the frontal eye fields (FEF), which sit - intuitively enough - in the frontal lobe. The FEF contains a retinotopic map: its cortical layout preserves the spatial arrangement of the retina, so a location in the visual world has an address in the tissue. Stimulate two retinal spots, A and B (with B to the right of A), and the FEF patch excited by B lies to the right of the patch excited by A.
The map is not just for looking at things. Artificially stimulate FEF cells in a monkey and its eyes jump to exactly the location in space that patch of tissue represents.

steps.prompt: Electrically stimulate a patch of a monkey's FEF strongly, and its eyes jump to the exact location that patch represents. Predict what happens when you stimulate the same patch too weakly to trigger any eye movement.
steps.reveal: Moore and Fallah (2001) found the eyes stay put - but the monkey becomes measurably better at detecting targets at precisely that location. Covert attention was deployed there. The circuitry that aims the eyes doubles as the circuitry that aims attention, and driving it below the eye-movement threshold still enhances sensory processing at the represented spot - control signals causing enhancement, demonstrated with a wire.

steps.body:
When control regions fail, attention fails in recognizable shapes. Damage to the right parietal lobe can produce visual neglect: because vision is processed contralaterally, patients fail to notice their entire left visual field - asked to copy a drawing, they leave out much of the left side of each object. Yet they are not blind there: an exogenous cue can still drag their awareness into the neglected field, and then they see and describe what is there. Curiously, left parietal damage does not typically cause right neglect - the right parietal lobe can generate attention to both fields and pitches in.
In ADHD, go/no-go studies find that frontoparietal regions are activated inefficiently when a prepared button-press must be suppressed, producing more no-go errors (Durston et al., 2003) - a dysregulation of attention-control networks, not a sensory defect.

steps.q: After right parietal damage, a patient copies drawings but omits much of the left side of every object. Yet when something flashes in her left visual field, she turns, sees it, and describes it accurately. What does this pattern show?
options: Her deficit is attentional, not visual - the damaged parietal lobe fails to direct attention into the left field, though vision there is intact
She is blind in the left visual field, so no cue could ever reach her
Her visual cortex no longer receives any left-field information
She has simply forgotten what the left sides of familiar objects look like
steps.explain: The exogenous cue is the giveaway: if the left field were truly blind or unrepresented, a flash there could not capture her awareness. Vision is delivering the data; the damaged right parietal lobe is failing to allocate attention to it - visual neglect is a disorder of attentional control, not sight.

title: Memory: the core machinery
blurb: Encoding, storage, retrieval, capacity, duration, and the modal-model map.

steps.body:
Memory connects past information to present cognition.
Memory is the use of information obtained in the past to generate a cognitive function now. That requires three linked processes: encoding creates a nervous-system representation, storage maintains it beyond immediate processing, and retrieval accesses it for a purpose. If information is never encoded, it cannot later be remembered.

steps.prompt: You hear a code, keep it available for several seconds, then call it back to type it. Which sequence best describes what happened?
choices: Retrieval → storage → encoding
Encoding → storage → retrieval
Storage → rehearsal → sensation
Attention → decay → interference
steps.reveal: The code must first be encoded, then remain stored, and finally be retrieved when you type it.

steps.body:
Memory systems are compared on two independent dimensions.
Capacity asks how much a system can hold. Duration asks how long information remains. A system can have a small capacity and brief duration, while another can hold far more for much longer. The claim that multiple memory systems have different properties rests on experiments, behavioral recordings, and observational reports.

steps.prompt: Build the Atkinson-Shiffrin sequence from first contact with a stimulus to durable storage.
steps.reveal: Sensory input → sensory memory → short-term memory → long-term memory. Attention selects sensory information for STM; encoding sends STM information to LTM; retrieval brings LTM information back into STM. This is the Atkinson-Shiffrin model, also called the modal model or information-processing model. Its timeline is roughly 1 second for sensory memory, 15–30 seconds for unrehearsed STM, and potentially lifelong storage in LTM.

steps.q: Which modal-model transition is correctly labeled?
options: Sensory memory → STM by attention
STM → sensory memory by encoding
LTM → sensory input by rehearsal
Sensory memory → LTM by retrieval
steps.explain: Attention selects part of the brief sensory trace and moves it into short-term memory.

steps.q: What distinction did the modal model make between STM and LTM?
options: STM supports current tasks; LTM supports durable storage
STM stores only visual input; LTM stores only auditory input
STM has unlimited duration; LTM lasts about one second
STM performs retrieval; LTM performs sensory transduction
steps.explain: The model separated temporary storage for current tasks from long-term storage that can persist across the lifespan.

title: The sensory-memory window
blurb: Why a rich sensory trace can be available for only an instant—and how Sperling proved it.

steps.body:
Sensory memory is a brief holding stage.
It retains information just encoded by the sensory organs before attention chooses what will enter short-term memory. The modal-model timeline places this store at roughly 1 second. Close your eyes after viewing a scene: for a moment the image seems present, then it rapidly fades.

steps.prompt: Why is sensory memory useful if it fades so quickly?
choices: It makes every sensory detail permanent
It briefly holds input for selection
It eliminates the need for short-term memory
It prevents retrieval from long-term memory
steps.reveal: Its value is the selection window: the trace holds long enough for attention to move chosen information into STM.

steps.body:
Sperling (1960) separated availability from report.
Participants briefly saw three rows of letters. In whole report, they tried to report the entire grid and produced about 25%, usually one row. In partial report, a high, medium, or low tone presented after the grid identified one row; participants reported about 75–80% of that row.

steps.prompt: The tone came after the grid disappeared, yet participants could report whichever row it selected. What does that imply?
steps.reveal: Most of the grid was briefly available in sensory memory. Whole report was low because the trace faded during the time needed to speak all the letters, not because only one row had been seen.

steps.q: What happened when Sperling increased the delay between the display and the row cue?
options: Recall increased because rehearsal improved
Recall stayed at 75–80% indefinitely
Recall fell as the sensory trace faded
Recall transferred directly into long-term memory
steps.explain: A longer display-to-tone delay left less of the rapidly fading sensory trace available.

steps.body: The logic: immediate partial report estimates how much was briefly available; declining performance across cue delays estimates how quickly that store disappears. Attention is the bridge from this rich but fleeting trace into STM.

title: How much fits in STM?
blurb: Auditory span, visual capacity, resource limits, and the power of meaningful chunks.

steps.body:
Short-term memory holds attended information for current use.
Without active maintenance, information typically lasts about 15–30 seconds. Repeating a newly heard phone number keeps it active long enough to use or encode.

steps.prompt: Miller presented ordered lists of letters, numbers, or words for immediate repetition. What stable auditory span did he report?
choices: About 1 item
About 4–5 items
About 7 ± 2 items
An unlimited number
steps.reveal: Miller's classic estimate was about 7 ± 2 auditory items, with reliable individual differences.

steps.body:
Visual STM has its own limit.
In change detection, a participant sees objects such as colored squares, then judges whether a second display is identical or changed. The data suggest a capacity of roughly 4–5 visual items. A resource-pool figure also shows fewer items retained as each item becomes more complex.

steps.prompt: Why can 1776 1492 2001 2018 be easier than 1776149220012018 even though both contain the same digits?
steps.reveal: Recognizable years allow chunking: long-term knowledge turns many digits into a few meaningful wholes, reducing the number of STM units. This is why Miller's auditory limit is best understood as roughly 7 ± 2 chunks, not necessarily 7 ± 2 individual digits.

steps.q: What did Chase and Simon's chess result show about expert memory?
options: Experts had unlimited memory for both real and random boards
Experts led on meaningful boards, not random ones
Novices recalled meaningful positions better than experts
Random boards created larger chunks than game positions
steps.explain: Experts used learned chess configurations as chunks. Random arrangements removed the meaningful patterns that supported the advantage.

steps.q: What best explains the apparent 'super-memory' of a professional mnemonist?
options: A greatly expanded basic STM capacity
A sensory trace that never decays
They form large meaningful chunks
The absence of any long-term knowledge
steps.explain: Exceptional string recall reflects chunking skill, not a fundamentally larger item limit.

title: Why short-term memories disappear
blurb: Rehearsal, the Brown-Peterson task, decay, interference, and the experiment that separated time from competition.

steps.body:
Rehearsal changes STM duration.
Rehearsal repeats information and reactivates its encoding, so information can theoretically remain active as long as rehearsal continues. To measure duration without rehearsal, the Brown-Peterson task presented a trigram and then forced participants to count backward by threes.

steps.prompt: Why did counting backward by threes matter in the Brown-Peterson task?
choices: It created meaningful chunks
It blocked rehearsal
It cued one row of letters
It moved the trigram into LTM
steps.reveal: The counting task occupied the process participants would otherwise use to repeat the trigram. Under distraction, recall suggested about a 15-second unrehearsed duration.

steps.body:
Two explanations compete.
Decay says information is lost simply as time passes. Interference says competing information displaces it. Proactive interference carries earlier information forward to disrupt later learning; retroactive interference lets newer information disrupt older material.

steps.prompt: Why did Keppel and Underwood focus on the first few trials of the Peterson task?
steps.reveal: Early trials contain little buildup from prior trigrams. Recall stayed fairly high for up to about 15 seconds there, showing that proactive interference contributed to the later forgetting curve. Considering later trials left room for both interference and decay.

steps.q: Lewandowsky et al. blocked rehearsal with articulatory suppression and varied recall speed. Recall did not worsen at slower speeds. What follows?
options: Time alone caused no decay without interference
Slower recall always strengthens sensory memory
Articulatory suppression creates long-term storage
Only retroactive interference can affect letters
steps.explain: If elapsed time alone caused forgetting, slower output should have reduced recall. It did not, so the study argued against pure time-based decay.

steps.body:
Keep the studies straight.
Peterson's curve first looked like decay. Keppel and Underwood showed that prior trials created proactive interference. Lewandowsky isolated the passage of time more carefully and found no speed effect. The decay-versus-interference question is therefore an empirical design problem, not a definition to memorize in isolation.

title: Working memory as an active system
blurb: Specialized stores, executive filtering, the episodic buffer, individual differences, and training claims.

steps.body:
Baddeley replaced a passive box with an active workspace.
The visuo-spatial sketchpad holds and manipulates visual information. The phonological loop repeats and analyzes auditory information. The central executive coordinates the two stores and controls what enters working memory.

steps.prompt: Match each task to its best component: mentally rotate a shape; silently repeat a sentence; switch attention between the two.
steps.reveal: Mental rotation → visuo-spatial sketchpad. Repeating the sentence → phonological loop. Coordinating and switching → central executive.

steps.body:
Brooks (1968) tested separate memory codes.
Participants completed verbal or visual-memory tasks using either spoken yes/no responses or pointing on a visual grid. The visual diagram task slowed dramatically with the visual pointing response, supporting distinct auditory/verbal and visual buffers with modality-specific competition.

steps.q: Which Brooks result most strongly supports a separate visual working-memory code?
options: The visual task slowed most with visual pointing
Every task was equally fast with every response mode
The verbal task could not be completed with speech
Participants remembered random chess boards perfectly
steps.explain: The large within-modality cost is what a separate, capacity-limited visual code predicts.

steps.body:
The central executive protects limited space.
In Vogel et al. (2005), high- and low-capacity participants remembered blue rectangles while red rectangles sometimes acted as distractors. With targets alone, both groups' ERP activity tracked two versus four items. With distractors, low-capacity participants showed a strong load response, while high-capacity participants showed a weaker response—evidence that filtering helps determine apparent capacity. The same idea applies to some age-related decline. Processing speed, working memory, and LTM decline with age while world knowledge is more preserved; aging also brings lower total gray-matter volume and less elaborate neural structure. High literacy or numeracy use tracks better skill maintenance than low use across age-skill profiles.

steps.prompt: Why was an episodic buffer added if the visual and auditory stores are separate?
choices: To erase long-term memories during a task
To bind visual, auditory, and LTM into an episode
To replace the central executive with sensory memory
To store only speech without a time limit
steps.reveal: The episodic buffer is a time-limited store controlled by the central executive. It binds the specialized stores with long-term knowledge into a multisensory, time-based representation.

steps.q: Which statement best captures the evidence on individual differences and brain training?
options: Working-memory capacity is unrelated to reasoning or mathematics
Training never improves performance on working-memory tasks
WM correlates with g; broad training transfer is unclear
Any commercial app has proven permanent gains across all cognition
steps.explain: Working-memory capacity correlates with g and skills such as math and reasoning. Musical training has been linked with improved WM in young children, and WM practice can improve trained performance, but wide transfer claims remain controversial.

title: The neural evidence for working memory
blurb: Distributed modality networks, sustained prefrontal activity, human imaging, and lesion evidence.

steps.body:
Working memory is distributed.
It begins with perceptual encoding and continues while information is actively maintained. Cabeza and Nyberg's meta-analysis found no single working-memory region. Auditory tasks recruit auditory areas such as temporal cortex; visual tasks recruit visual areas such as occipital cortex. Frontal regions are especially important for executive demands.

steps.prompt: How can it be true both that 'working memory happens all over the brain' and that 'the frontal lobe is especially important'?
steps.reveal: Modality-specific regions represent the content, while frontal regions contribute strongly to active maintenance and executive control. A distributed system can still have a particularly important control region.

steps.body:
Funahashi et al. (1989) recorded prefrontal neurons.
A neuron that responded to a square's location fired strongly during the delay when a monkey had to remember that location. The sustained delay response disappeared when no memory task was required, tying the activity to active maintenance rather than the stimulus alone.

steps.q: What human result from Schon et al. (2008) paralleled Funahashi's delay activity?
options: Prefrontal activity rose during the memory delay
Temporal activity vanished while participants listened to speech
Occipital damage improved delayed matching
A cue tone increased sensory-memory duration
steps.explain: In a delayed-match-to-sample task, human prefrontal activity increased during the period when the first image had to be maintained.

steps.body:
Activation shows association; damage tests necessity more directly.
Moore et al. (2010) found that damage to dorsolateral prefrontal cortex impaired tasks similar to delayed matching. Because frontal lobes support executive function, this region may contribute to the central executive.

steps.q: Why is the Moore lesion finding stronger causal evidence than activation alone?
options: Damage impaired working-memory performance
The region became active during every sensory event
The study proved all memory is stored in one neuron
The task removed every executive demand
steps.explain: When disruption of a region accompanies loss of function, the evidence more directly supports a necessary contribution than a correlation from activity alone.

title: Memory systems through amnesia
blurb: Use H.M., Clive Wearing, and K.F. to separate short-term and long-term memory.

steps.body:
STM and LTM differ in more than duration.
Short-term memory briefly retains specific stimulus details, usually for about 15–30 seconds. Long-term memory can retain abstracted semantic information indefinitely, but stored information must remain retrievable.

Put amnesia on a timeline.
Retrograde amnesia removes access to events before a neurological event. Anterograde amnesia impairs memory for new information encountered afterward. A person can show either pattern or both.

steps.prompt: A patient remembers childhood but repeatedly forgets conversations held after an injury. Which pattern is most direct?
choices: Retrograde amnesia
Anterograde amnesia
A primacy effect
A procedural-memory advantage
steps.reveal: The missing information was encountered after the event, so this is anterograde amnesia.

steps.body:
H.M. and Clive Wearing preserved islands of function.
After hippocampal surgery, H.M. retained identity, general knowledge, and immediate memory but could not form new LTM. Wearing had severe retrograde and anterograde amnesia yet retained brief STM, language, piano skill, and basic facts.

steps.prompt: Why is Patient K.F.—new LTM formation with an STM span of only two or three items—especially valuable evidence?
choices: K.F. exactly duplicates H.M.'s deficit
K.F. shows that rehearsal is unnecessary
K.F. supplies the reverse STM-LTM pattern
K.F. proves all memory is hippocampal
steps.reveal: H.M. preserved STM but lost new LTM; K.F. impaired STM but preserved new LTM. The crossed pattern supports distinct systems.

steps.q: Which observation most strongly argues that STM and LTM rely on distinguishable mechanisms?
options: Every patient forgets both recent and remote events equally
H.M. and K.F. show opposite preservation-and-impairment patterns
The final items in every list are recalled better than the middle
Category cues improve recall compared with an unguided search
steps.explain: Opposing dissociations show that one memory system can function when the other is impaired.

title: Encoding succeeds only when retrieval works
blurb: Connect rehearsal, serial position, processing depth, transfer, and encoding specificity.

steps.body:
Rehearsal is not all equal.
Maintenance rehearsal repeats information without added thought. Elaborative rehearsal considers meaning and is more effective at moving information toward LTM.

The serial-position curve reveals two mechanisms.
Early items benefit from rehearsal and LTM—the primacy effect. Final items remain active in STM—the recency effect. A 30-second delay removes recency.

steps.prompt: A delay after the last word erases the end-of-list advantage. What does that imply?
choices: Recency normally depends on STM
Primacy normally depends on STM
Every list item was semantically encoded
Category cues caused the original curve
steps.reveal: The final items lose their advantage when they are no longer active in STM.

steps.body:
Depth helps—but match can win.
Craik and Tulving found best memory after meaning-based sentence completion. Morris showed that rhyme encoding can win when the test cue also asks for rhyme. Transfer-appropriate processing is the match between encoding and retrieval operations.

Cues recover what an unguided search may miss.
